==Problem 24==

The notation <imath>n!</imath> (read "n factorial") is defined as the product of the first <imath>n</imath> positive integers. (For example, <imath>3!=1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 6</imath>). Define the superfactorial of a positive integer, denoted by <imath>n^!</imath>, to be the product of the factorials of the first <imath>n</imath> integers. (For example, <imath>3^!=1! \cdot 2! \cdot 3! = 12</imath>). How many factors of <imath>7</imath> appear in the prime factorization of <imath>51^!</imath>, the superfactorial of <imath>51</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 147 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 150 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 156 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 168 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 171</imath>

==Solution 1 (Solution 2 simplified) - Come and Go Solution==

From <imath> 7! - 13! </imath>, there is one power of <imath> 7 </imath>. From <imath> 14! - 20! </imath>, there are <imath> 2 </imath> powers. <imath> 21! - 27! </imath>, <imath> 3 </imath> powers. <imath> 28! - 34! </imath>, <imath> 4 </imath> powers. From <imath> 35! - 41! </imath>, <imath> 5 </imath> powers. From <imath> 42! - 48! </imath>, <imath> 6 </imath> powers. Finally, from <imath> 49! </imath> to <imath> 51! </imath>, there are <imath> 8 </imath> powers (as each one contributes <imath>7^2</imath>). Thus, in a superfactorial, the number of powers is just <imath> 7+14+21+28+35+42+24 </imath> powers total, or <imath> \boxed{171} </imath>.

~Pinotation

In another way, we can think of it like 7 multiples. For example, from seven to thirteen there happens to exist 7 7's. Later from 14 to 20 there happens to exist 7*2 sevens. When we continue to move on to 49 and 51, there exists an extra seven because of the squares. Adding them up we should get 171 as our answer.

Note for Jellycat88: That logic is flawed. Definition of multiples always implies one factor of seven. your idea works as long as the value is not a perfect square. for instance, <imath>14!</imath> through <imath>21!</imath>, each corresponds two multiples of seven, those being 7 and 14. when you count that extra square, you are counting a power not a multiple, because from 49 to 51, we obtain only seven multiples, 7,14,21,28,35,42,49. However, from 49 through 51, we obtain eight '''powers'''. it is a minor yet huge difference, which is why your logic is slightly flawed.

~Pinotation

==Solution 2 - Thought Process==

We begin by noticing that for the first few factorials (<imath>1!</imath> to <imath>6!</imath>) there are no factors of <imath>7</imath>, because the first multiple of <imath>7</imath> is <imath>7</imath> itself. So, these numbers contribute <imath>0</imath> sevens.

The next <imath>7</imath> factorials (<imath>7!</imath> to <imath>13!</imath>) all have one factor of <imath>7</imath> in them, since every number less than or equal to <imath>n</imath> is multiplied in <imath>n!</imath>. These all contribute <imath>7</imath> sevens.

For the next <imath>7</imath> factorials (<imath>14!</imath> to <imath>20!</imath>), there are two factors of <imath>7</imath> (namely <imath>7</imath> and <imath>14</imath>). These numbers contribute <imath>14</imath> sevens.

If we continue with this method, we see that once we hit <imath>7k!</imath> we have <imath>7k</imath> sevens contributed, since there are <imath>7</imath> numbers in between. This will work from <imath>1!</imath> to <imath>48!</imath>, because when we get to <imath>49! = (7^2)!</imath>, we have one extra <imath>7</imath> for every number, since we have an extra factor of <imath>7</imath>.

This is only for <imath>3</imath> numbers, <imath>49!</imath>, <imath>50!</imath>, and <imath>51!</imath> (our final factorial). They have <imath>7+1 = 8</imath> factors of <imath>7</imath>, because they have <imath>7</imath> multiples of <imath>7</imath> and one extra from <imath>49</imath>. These three contribute a total of <imath>3 \cdot 8 = 24</imath> sevens.

Finally, sum these numbers. Most are just the first <imath>6</imath> multiples of <imath>7</imath>, and we can calculate this sum to be <imath>0 + 7 + 14 + 21 + \dots + 42 = 7 \cdot \frac{6(6+1)}{2} = 7 \cdot \frac{42}{2} = 7 \cdot 21 = 147</imath>. The final step is to add the final <imath>3\cdot 8 = 24</imath> sevens to get our answer, <imath>147 + 24 = \boxed{ \textbf{(E) } 171}</imath>.

~OlympiadMaster

==Solution 3==

If <imath>51^! = 1! \cdot 2! \cdot ... \cdot 51! = (1) (1 \cdot 2)(1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3)(...)(1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot ... \cdot 51)</imath> is expanded as such, each integer <imath>k \leq 51</imath> will appear once in each of the expansions of <imath>\{k!, ..., 51!\}</imath>, for a total of <imath>52-k</imath> appearances.  

Therefore, in this expansion, <imath>7</imath> appears <imath>45</imath> times, <imath>14</imath> appears <imath>38</imath> times, <imath>21</imath> appears <imath>31</imath> times, <imath>28</imath> appears <imath>24</imath> times, <imath>35</imath> appears <imath>17</imath> times, <imath>42</imath> appears <imath>10</imath> times, and <imath>49</imath> appears <imath>3</imath> times.  Except for <imath>49</imath>, which contributes <imath>2</imath> copies of the factor <imath>7</imath>, each of these terms contributes <imath>1</imath> copy of the factor <imath>7</imath>, for a total of <imath>45 + 38 + 31 + 24 + 17 + 10 + 3 \cdot 2 = \boxed{ \textbf{(E) } 171}</imath> copies of the factor <imath>7</imath>.


-j314andrews

== Solution 4 ==

We can count how many multiples of <imath>7</imath> appear throughout the expression. The number <imath>7</imath> appears from <imath>7!</imath> to <imath>51!</imath>, for a total of <imath>51 - 7 + 1 = 45</imath> times. The number <imath>14</imath> appears from <imath>14!</imath> to <imath>51!</imath>, for a total of <imath>51 - 14 + 1 = 38</imath> times. 

If we continue this, we find that the total is the sum of numbers decreasing by <imath>7</imath> each time: 
<cmath>45 + 38 + 31 + 24 + 17 + 10 + 3 = 168</cmath>

Since <imath>49 = 7^2</imath>, we count an extra <imath>7</imath> in <imath>49!</imath>, <imath>50!</imath>, and <imath>51!</imath>. Adding these three extra factors gives:
<cmath>168 + 3 = \mathbf{171}</cmath>

Therefore, the final answer is <imath>\boxed{\text{(E) 171}}</imath>.

~Frigate
